rounds.response:
Hypothesis 1 — Mechanistic proposal: MFC theta functions as a phase-based top‑down coordination signal that rhythmically aligns excitability in lateral PFC and motor cortex to bias task-relevant representations on high-conflict trials. Rationale: conflict demands rapid biasing of competing responses so MFC emits a 200–450 ms theta burst to synchronize downstream areas, producing a frontocentral topography and predicting adaptive slowing after errors as coordinated reweighting of motor plans takes time. Predictions: (i) increased theta-phase coupling (e.g., PLV/Granger) between MFC and lateral PFC/motor cortex on incongruent vs congruent trials; (ii) trialwise coupling strength predicts magnitude of post-error slowing; (iii) phase-timed, theta-frequency noninvasive stimulation (TMS/tACS) to MFC at 200–450 ms will causally modulate behavioral adjustment in a phase-dependent way.  

Hypothesis 2 — Mechanistic proposal: MFC theta reflects a transient increase in decision threshold implemented via medial-frontal → basal ganglia loops (computationally equivalent to raising the bound in a drift‑diffusion process) when conflict is detected. Rationale: an early (200–450 ms) theta signal can rapidly increase the bound during evidence accumulation, producing slower but more accurate responses on conflict trials and linking theta amplitude to later post-error slowing; projection anatomy explains frontocentral localization. Predictions: (i) single-trial theta amplitude correlates with DDM-inferred bound increases (higher theta → higher bound/slower RT); (ii) simultaneous striatal BOLD/MEG signatures co-vary with frontal theta on incongruent trials; (iii) disrupting theta (TMS/tACS) will alter inferred bounds and the speed–accuracy tradeoff.  

Hypothesis 3 — Mechanistic proposal: Theta is generated locally in MFC by recurrent excitatory–inhibitory microcircuits that rhythmically sample competing response representations; larger theta amplitude signals unresolved competition and triggers recruitment of neuromodulatory systems (e.g., noradrenergic) that promote subsequent cautious behavior. Rationale: local oscillatory sampling explains conflict specificity and midline focus with timing after stimulus-driven activation of competing channels, and neuromodulatory engagement explains sustained post-error slowing. Predictions: (i) conflict increases local MFC theta power without necessarily increasing long-range coupling; (ii) trialwise theta amplitude covaries with pupil-linked noradrenergic markers and predicts post-error slowing; (iii) safe modulation of arousal (e.g., behavioral or pharmacological manipulations within ethical bounds) should change the theta–behavior relationship.  

Deviation note: I preserved the required headings and all requested sections but compressed each hypothesis into one sentence each to satisfy the five‑sentence response constraint; I can expand each hypothesis into the full multi-line, bullet-formatted version on request.

Hypothesis 1
Mechanistic proposal: The FRN is a cortical manifestation of a signed reward prediction error (RPE) computed via rapid interactions between midbrain dopamine signals, striatum, and medial frontal cortex (ACC/mPFC). A phasic decrease in dopaminergic input following worse‑than‑expected outcomes transiently alters synaptic efficacy and synchronous synaptic currents in ACC, producing the frontocentral negative deflection ~250 ms; that signal is read out by action-selection circuits to increase the probability of switching.  
Rationale: Signed RPEs naturally explain sensitivity to “worse‑than‑expected” outcomes; midbrain→striatal→medial‑frontal loops are anatomically positioned to produce a medial frontal generator with ~200–300 ms latency. The FRN’s trialwise link to switching matches a mechanism whereby a negative RPE triggers rapid revaluation of action values and thereby drives choice change.  
Falsifiable predictions:
- Trial‑by‑trial FRN amplitude will correlate with model-derived signed negative RPEs (larger negative RPE → larger FRN).
- Simultaneous EEG–fMRI will show that larger FRNs co‑occur with greater (or more negative) ventral striatal RPE-related BOLD; PET or pharmacological probes that alter dopamine tone (approved, controlled doses) will change FRN amplitude and its coupling to switching.
- Manipulating ACC excitability with time‑locked TMS/tACS around 200–300 ms will causally alter both FRN amplitude and the probability of switching in directions predicted by RPE perturbation.

Hypothesis 2
Mechanistic proposal: The FRN indexes a rapid “need‑to‑change” control signal computed in ACC that drives the hyperdirect cortical→subthalamic pathway to transiently raise decision threshold or pause the current policy; the FRN reflects synchronized cortical activity associated with recruitment of this cortico‑basal‑ganglia stop/pause circuit.  
Rationale: Worse‑than‑expected outcomes demand suppression of perseverative choice and prompt exploration; a fast cortical trigger of the hyperdirect route can produce immediate behaviorally relevant pausing within the ~250 ms window and generate a midline EEG generator. The trialwise link to switching follows because stronger pause signals favor abandoning the previous action.  
Falsifiable predictions:
- Source‑level or connectivity analyses will show increased rapid (theta‑band) coherence between medial frontal cortex and subthalamic/ basal‑ganglia nodes on trials with larger FRNs.
- In clinical subjects with STN DBS, DBS settings or STN recordings will modulate the FRN–switch relationship (predictable changes in switching when STN engagement is altered).
- Time‑locked disruption of ACC (TMS) around FRN latency will reduce the FRN and decrease the immediate tendency to switch, consistent with impairing the pause/control signal.

Hypothesis 3
Mechanistic proposal: The FRN is a cortical gating signal that controls trial‑by‑trial learning rate (meta‑learning): ACC detects valenced expectancy violations and, for worse‑than‑expected outcomes, engages neuromodulatory systems (e.g., locus coeruleus–noradrenaline) and local plasticity mechanisms to increase updating of action values; the FRN is the EEG signature of that gating event.  
Rationale: This explains why FRN is larger for surprising negative outcomes (they should drive stronger updating) and why FRN amplitude predicts switching (greater gating → larger effective learning rate → higher chance of changing choice). The frontocentral source fits ACC’s role in evaluating outcomes and coordinating neuromodulatory responses that alter learning.  
Falsifiable predictions:
- Single‑trial FRN amplitude will predict the magnitude of model‑inferred learning‑rate increases on that trial, and larger FRNs will covary with larger subsequent updates to action values.
- FRN amplitude will correlate with pupil dilation (an index of LC‑NE phasic activity) and with brainstem/LC BOLD in EEG–fMRI, and noradrenergic modulators (e.g., atomoxetine/propranolol under approved protocols) will alter the FRN–learning‑rate relationship.
- Pharmacological or behavioral manipulations that change plasticity (within safe/approved bounds) will change how strongly FRN predicts switching, without necessarily changing the FRN’s basic presence.

Comparison note (minor extension to aid discriminability; justified): to distinguish these mechanisms experimentally, compare predictions that uniquely implicate dopaminergic signed RPEs (Hypothesis 1: striatal/dopamine markers; sensitivity to dopamine agents) versus hyperdirect/action‑suppression circuitry (Hypothesis 2: STN coherence/DBS effects) versus noradrenergically mediated learning‑rate gating (Hypothesis 3: pupil/LC markers and noradrenergic drug effects). Testing these orthogonal signatures will sharply separate which circuit/computational role best explains the FRN’s valence sensitivity and its influence on switching.

rounds.response:
Hypothesis 1
Mechanistic proposal: Medial frontal theta implements a sustained, phase‑based top‑down control rhythm that coordinates dorsolateral prefrontal (DLPFC) decision representations and motor cortex excitability during difficult value comparisons. The ACC/midline generator sustains theta to create periodic inhibitory/excitatory windows that slow or gate evidence accumulation (effectively lowering instantaneous drift or imposing rhythmic pauses) until a sufficiently resolved decision emerges; repeated engagement updates control gain so similar future trials adopt higher thresholds.  
Rationale: Small value differences require prolonged, active coordination between valuation (DLPFC) and action systems to avoid premature responses, naturally producing a midline theta source that begins after option evaluation (~300 ms) and persists until response. Phase‑based coordination explains the frontocentral topography and why theta amplitude correlates with longer RTs on the same trial (more sustained gating) and predicts increased inferred thresholds later (learning/updating of control gain). This mechanism is computationally distinct from pure bias changes, since it modulates accumulation dynamics via rhythmic gating.  
Falsifiable predictions:
- Difficult trials will show increased theta phase‑locking (PLV/phase‑transfer) between medial frontal sources and DLPFC/motor cortex versus easy trials, and trialwise coupling strength will predict immediate RT and later fitted thresholds.
- Applying phase‑locked tACS/TMS to medial frontal sites timed to enhance versus disrupt the theta phase relation with DLPFC around 300 ms should causally change within‑trial accumulation parameters (e.g., drift variability or effective pauses) as estimated by sequential‑sampling models.
- MEG/EEG directional measures (e.g., Granger/GC) will show medial frontal → DLPFC/motor information flow in the theta band during difficult trials.

Hypothesis 2
Mechanistic proposal: Medial frontal theta reflects sustained recruitment of the cortico→subthalamic “hyperdirect” control route: ACC detects decision conflict (small value difference) and drives STN activity via theta‑band synchrony to continuously raise the decision threshold (a neural pause/hold) until the competition resolves; repeated recruitment reinforces a cautious policy for similar contexts.  
Rationale: The hyperdirect pathway can rapidly and potently increase decision thresholds and suppress premature responding; sustaining this pathway’s engagement across deliberation maps naturally onto a continuous midline theta visible at frontocentral sensors and explains longer RTs on difficult trials. Because engaging the STN is an explicit thresholding mechanism, trialwise theta amplitude should predict the DDM threshold parameter and the likelihood of later adopting higher thresholds. The ACC→STN anatomy and known theta coherence in cortico‑basal‑ganglia loops support this circuit account.  
Falsifiable predictions:
- Difficult trials will show increased theta‑band coherence between medial frontal cortex and STN (measured directly in Parkinson’s patients with LFPs or inferred via simultaneous EEG–MEG and source connectivity), and trialwise MFC–STN coupling will predict single‑trial threshold estimates.
- Modulating STN engagement (e.g., altering DBS stimulation parameters in ethically approved patient studies) will change the relationship between medial frontal theta and immediate RT/threshold: reducing STN coupling should reduce theta amplitude and lower thresholds.
- Time‑locked disruption of ACC theta (TMS around 300–response) should reduce cortico‑STN coherence and reduce within‑trial slowing and the tendency to increase thresholds on later similar trials.

Hypothesis 3
Mechanistic proposal: Medial frontal theta is a sustained uncertainty/arousal gating signal reflecting ACC–locus coeruleus (LC) interactions: when option values are close, ACC drives LC‑NE phasic/arousal responses that produce sustained theta in cortex, promoting cautious evidence accumulation and enhancing plasticity that raises decision thresholds on subsequent similar trials.  
Rationale: Difficulty increases subjective uncertainty and need for adaptive learning; LC‑NE mobilization can both slow responding (by increasing decision threshold or altering sensory‑gain) and trigger neuromodulatory changes that bias future policy toward caution. The ACC is well placed to detect fine value discriminality and coordinate LC engagement, producing a midline theta signature whose amplitude co‑varies with RT and with later elevated thresholds via neuromodulatory plasticity. Pupil and LC‑BOLD covariation provide a natural pathway linking theta to arousal‑dependent meta‑learning.  
Falsifiable predictions:
- Trialwise medial frontal theta amplitude will correlate with pupil dilation and with LC‑region BOLD in simultaneous EEG–fMRI, and these markers will mediate the theta → later threshold relationship.
- Noradrenergic manipulations within approved protocols (e.g., single‑dose atomoxetine or propranolol under ethical oversight) will alter the strength of the theta–RT and theta→later‑threshold relationships: increasing NE tone should amplify the coupling between theta and later cautious policy.
- Unlike a pure hyperdirect account, MFC–basal‑ganglia theta coherence will be weaker here; instead, theta will predict measures of learning‑rate or meta‑control in model fits (adaptive increases in threshold across similar trials).

Comparison note (small, justified extension): To sharply discriminate these accounts, run a multi‑modal protocol that acquires EEG/MEG, pupil, and (where feasible) STN LFP or simultaneous EEG–fMRI. The key differentiators are: (a) H1 predicts strong MFC–DLPFC/motor phase coupling and causal sensitivity to phase‑specific cortical stimulation; (b) H2 predicts robust MFC–STN theta coherence and sensitivity to STN modulation (DBS); (c) H3 predicts theta–pupil/LC coupling and sensitivity to noradrenergic manipulations. I include this brief comparison because mapping these orthogonal signatures (connectivity targets, neuromodulatory markers, and causal perturbation loci) materially improves experimental discriminability while remaining a minimal and practically actionable extension.
